title: Better without children
translation: Whether you're of high birth or a nobody, it's better not to have children.

Prince Kaneakira, Nobunaga and Arihito all hoped their family line would die out. The old storyteller in The Great Mirror says it was a good thing that Yoshifusa had no descendants, because descendants who turn out badly are a bad thing. And when Prince Shōtoku had his tomb built in advance, he is supposed to have said: "Cut it off here, sever it there. I don't want any descendants."
original: {我|わ}が{身|み}のやんごとなからむにも、まして{数|かず}ならざらむにも、{子|こ}といふもの{無|な}くてありなむ。
{前中書王|さきのちゆうしよわう}、{九条太政大臣|くでうのだいじやうだいじん}、{花園左大臣|はなぞののさだいじん}、{皆|みな}{族|ぞう}{絶|た}えむ{事|こと}を{願|ねが}ひ{給|たま}へり。
{染殿大臣|そめどののおとど}も{子孫|しそん}おはせぬぞよく{侍|はべ}る。
{末|すゑ}の{後|おく}れ{給|たま}へるは、わろき{事|こと}なりとぞ、{世継|よつぎ}の{翁|おきな}の{物語|ものがたり}にはいへる。
{聖徳太子|しやうとくたいし}の{御|み}{墓|はか}を、かねて{築|つ}かせ{給|たま}ひける{時|とき}も、「ここをきれ、かしこを{断|た}て。{子孫|しそん}あらせじと{思|おも}ふなり。」と{侍|はべ}りけるとかや。
literal: Whether one is of high rank, or, even more, of no account, it is surely better to be without children.
The former Prince of the Ministry of Central Affairs, the Kujō Chancellor and the Hanazono Minister of the Left all wished that their line would die out.
That the Somedono Minister had no descendants was also good.
That descendants fall behind (their ancestors) is a bad thing: so it says in the tale of old man Yotsugi.
Also when Prince Shōtoku had his tomb built in advance, he said, 'Cut here, sever there. It is because I do not want there to be descendants', or so they say.

notes.quote: 子といふもの無くてありなむ
notes.text: なむ here is ぬ (strong) + む: 'it would surely be better'. Kenkō was a priest, and there is no record that he had children; the section is a short argument for his own choice, backed up with famous names.

notes.quote: 前中書王、九条太政大臣、花園左大臣
notes.text: Three high nobles named by their titles, as people did at the time: Prince Kaneakira (914–987), Fujiwara no Nobunaga (1022–1094) and Minamoto no Arihito (1103–1147). The translation uses their names, because the titles mean nothing to a reader today.

The Ōkagami, 'The Great Mirror', a history of the Fujiwara told by an old man called Yotsugi. The Ōkagami itself says the opposite about Yoshifusa: it is a pity that he had no children. Kenkō probably remembered it wrong.
Fujiwara no Yoshifusa (804–872), the first regent who was not of imperial blood. He had a daughter but no son, and adopted his nephew.

notes.quote: 末の後れ給へるは、わろき事なり
notes.text: {後|おく}る: 'to fall behind'. The fear is not dying out, but having descendants who do not live up to their ancestors.

Prince Shōtoku (574–622), an early patron of Buddhism in Japan. The story comes from a legendary biography of him. The cutting is probably about the shape of the land around the tomb: in geomancy, a 'cut' in the ridge would cut off the family line. Twenty years after his death, his family was in fact destroyed in a political struggle (643).
'…or so they say'. Kenkō marks the story as hearsay.
